P.title: P.blurb
Electronics: Components and signals for tinkering with microcontrollers.

P.title: tr-parts.summary
Electronics: Resistors, LEDs, capacitors and the voltage divider: the parts in every maker kit.

P.title: tr-parts.q0.q
Electronics: A white LED (Vf 3 V) runs from 12 V at 10 mA. Which resistor?

P.title: tr-parts.q0.x
Electronics: R = (12 − 3) ÷ 0.010 = 900 Ω. You'd pick the next standard value up, 1 kΩ.

P.title: tr-parts.q1.q
Electronics: Bands brown, black, orange. What's the value?

P.title: tr-parts.q2.q
Electronics: In a divider with R1 = R2 and Vin = 10 V, Vout is…

P.title: tr-parts.q2.x
Electronics: Equal resistors split the voltage in half.

P.title: tr-parts.q3.q
Electronics: Two 1 kΩ resistors in parallel give…

P.title: tr-parts.q3.x
Electronics: Equal resistors in parallel halve the value.

P.title: tr-parts.q4.q
Electronics: What happens if you connect an electrolytic capacitor backwards?

P.title: tr-parts.c0.text
Electronics: Resistors are labelled with coloured bands. The first two are digits, the third is a multiplier, and a gold or silver band at the end gives the tolerance.\n\nBlack 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9.

P.title: tr-parts.c1.text
Electronics: An LED drops a fixed forward voltage (Vf, about 2 V for red, 3 V for white or blue) and will draw as much current as it can get, then burn out. A series resistor takes up the leftover voltage and sets the current.

P.title: tr-parts.c1.example.0
Electronics: 5 V supply, red LED (2 V), 20 mA

P.title: tr-parts.c2.text
Electronics: A capacitor is two plates separated by an insulator. Connect it to a voltage and charge piles up on the plates until it matches the supply. It charges quickly at first, then slows down.\n\nIn practice they smooth out ripples on a power rail and supply short bursts of current, which is why you see one next to almost every chip.

P.title: tr-parts.c3.text
Electronics: Two resistors in series split a voltage in proportion to their values. It's the standard way to bring a 5 V or 12 V signal down to the 3.3 V an ESP32 pin can take.

P.title: tr-parts.c4.text
Electronics: Resistors come in standard series rather than every value. The E12 series has 12 values per decade: 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82. Pick the nearest standard value to your calculation.

P.title: tr-parts.c5.text
Electronics: Resistors turn power into heat and have a maximum rating: common through-hole ones are ¼ W. Check P = I² × R and pick a resistor rated comfortably above it.

P.title: tr-parts.c5.example.2
Electronics: = 0.06 W: a ¼ W part is fine

P.title: tr-parts.c6.text
Electronics: In series, resistances add up. In parallel, the total is less than the smallest one; two equal resistors in parallel give half the value.

P.title: tr-parts.c7.text
Electronics: Ceramic capacitors are small and cheap, used for decoupling (typically 100 nF). Electrolytic capacitors store more (µF to mF) but are polarised: connect them backwards and they can burst.

P.title: tr-parts.c8.text
Electronics: A resistor charging a capacitor takes a predictable time. After one time constant (R × C) the capacitor reaches about 63% of the supply; after five, it's essentially full.

P.title: tr-parts.c9.text
Electronics: An inductor is a coil that resists changes in current, storing energy in its magnetic field. They're key in switching power supplies and filters.

P.title: tr-mcu.summary
Electronics: How a chip like the ESP32 reads and controls the real world.

P.title: tr-mcu.q0.q
Electronics: A 12 V motor gets PWM at 50% duty. It behaves roughly as if it had…

P.title: tr-mcu.q0.x
Electronics: The average of 12 V on half the time is 6 V.

P.title: tr-mcu.q1.o2
Electronics: Reads randomly because it picks up noise

P.title: tr-mcu.q1.x
Electronics: With nothing defining its level, the pin picks up stray charge. A pull-up or pull-down fixes that.

P.title: tr-mcu.q2.q
Electronics: How many steps does a 10-bit ADC have?

P.title: tr-mcu.q3.o1
Electronics: Because the contacts bounce and create several false presses

P.title: tr-mcu.q4.q
Electronics: What's the risk of putting 5 V into an ESP32 input pin?

P.title: tr-mcu.q4.o1
Electronics: It can damage the 3.3 V pin

P.title: tr-mcu.c0.text
Electronics: A digital signal has two states: low (0) or high (1, often 3.3 V). An analog signal can be any value in a range, like a temperature sensor's output.\n\nMicrocontrollers are digital at heart. To deal with analog they use an ADC to read and PWM to fake an output.

P.title: tr-mcu.c1.text
Electronics: Pulse-width modulation switches a pin fully on and off very fast. The fraction of time it's on is the duty cycle. An LED or motor responds to the average: 25% duty on a 12 V supply behaves roughly like 3 V.\n\nIt's efficient because the switch is always fully on or fully off, so little energy is wasted as heat.

P.title: tr-mcu.c2.text
Electronics: An input pin connected to nothing 'floats' and picks up noise, randomly reading 0 or 1. A pull-up resistor ties it gently to 3.3 V so it reads 1 by default. Press the button and the pin connects to ground, reading 0.\n\nMost microcontrollers have internal pull-ups you can switch on in code.

P.title: tr-mcu.c3.text
Electronics: An analog-to-digital converter turns a voltage into a number. An n-bit ADC has 2ⁿ steps. The ESP32's 12-bit ADC gives 4096 steps over about 3.3 V.\n\nIts readings are less accurate near 0 V and near the top of the range, so keep signals in the middle where you can.

P.title: tr-mcu.c4.text
Electronics: General-purpose input/output pins can be set as inputs (read a button) or outputs (drive an LED). On an ESP32 they work at 3.3 V and can safely supply only a few milliamps each.

P.title: tr-mcu.c5.text
Electronics: Many modern chips (ESP32, Raspberry Pi) use 3.3 V logic; Arduino Uno uses 5 V. Feeding 5 V into a 3.3 V pin can damage it. Use a voltage divider or level shifter between them.

P.title: tr-mcu.c5.viz.items.1.w
Electronics: 3.3 V pin drives a 5 V relay coil

P.title: tr-mcu.c6.text
Electronics: Instead of checking a button thousands of times a second (polling), an interrupt makes the chip jump to your code the moment the pin changes. It saves power and never misses a quick event.

P.title: tr-mcu.c7.text
Electronics: Mechanical buttons bounce: one press produces several rapid on-off pulses in a few milliseconds. Software ignores changes for ~20–50 ms after the first one, or a small capacitor smooths them.

P.title: tr-mcu.c7.viz.steps.1
Electronics: Contacts bounce for a few ms

P.title: tr-mcu.c8.text
Electronics: Rather than freezing the program with delay(), good code checks elapsed time and does other work meanwhile. This keeps sensors, Wi-Fi and displays responsive.

P.title: tr-mcu.c8.viz.items.0.r
Electronics: check elapsed time and keep looping

P.title: tr-mcu.c9.text
Electronics: A microcontroller (ESP32, Arduino) runs one program directly on the hardware, boots instantly and uses milliwatts. A single-board computer (Raspberry Pi) runs Linux, with more power and complexity.

P.title: tr-diodes.summary
Electronics: One-way valves for current, and their many uses.

P.title: tr-diodes.q0.q
Electronics: What does the band on a diode mark?

P.title: tr-diodes.q1.q
Electronics: Why fit a diode across a relay coil?

P.title: tr-diodes.q1.o1
Electronics: To absorb the voltage spike when it switches off

P.title: tr-diodes.q1.x
Electronics: The flyback diode protects the driver.

P.title: tr-diodes.q2.q
Electronics: Roughly what does a silicon diode drop when conducting?

P.title: tr-diodes.c0.text
Electronics: A diode lets current flow in one direction (anode to cathode) and blocks it the other way. The band on the body marks the cathode.

P.title: tr-diodes.c1.text
Electronics: A silicon diode drops about 0.6–0.7 V when conducting; a Schottky diode only 0.2–0.4 V, which wastes less power. LEDs drop more: 2 V for red, about 3 V for blue and white.

P.title: tr-diodes.c2.text
Electronics: A diode in series with a power input stops damage if someone connects the battery backwards. It costs a little voltage; a MOSFET does the same with almost no loss.

P.title: tr-diodes.c3.text
Electronics: Four diodes in a bridge turn AC into pulsing DC: both halves of the wave come out positive. Add a big capacitor and it smooths into near-steady DC.

P.title: tr-diodes.c4.text
Electronics: When you switch off a relay or motor coil, its magnetic field collapses and creates a voltage spike that can kill the transistor driving it. A diode across the coil safely absorbs the spike.

P.title: tr-diodes.c4.viz.items.0.r
Electronics: add a diode across the coil, band to +

P.title: tr-diodes.c4.viz.items.1.w
Electronics: transistor dies after a few weeks

P.title: tr-diodes.c5.text
Electronics: A Zener diode conducts backwards at a precise voltage, such as 3.3 V or 5.1 V. With a resistor it makes a simple voltage reference or protects inputs from overvoltage.

P.title: tr-diodes.c6.text
Electronics: A light-emitting diode gives off light when current flows forward. The colour depends on the semiconductor material. Long leg is the anode (+), the flat side marks the cathode (−).

P.title: tr-diodes.c7.text
Electronics: Run in reverse, a diode can detect light: photons free electrons and a tiny current flows. Light sensors, remote-control receivers and solar cells are all photodiodes at heart.

P.title: tr-diodes.c8.text
Electronics: Transient voltage suppressor diodes clamp very fast spikes, like static discharge on a USB port or a surge on a long sensor cable, protecting the chip behind them.

P.title: tr-diodes.c9.text
Electronics: Two diodes let a circuit run from whichever supply is higher, such as USB or a battery, without the two feeding into each other.

P.title: tr-transistors.summary
Electronics: How a tiny signal controls a big load.

P.title: tr-transistors.q0.q
Electronics: Why use a logic-level MOSFET with an ESP32?

P.title: tr-transistors.q0.o1
Electronics: It switches fully on with only 3.3 V on the gate

P.title: tr-transistors.q0.x
Electronics: Standard MOSFETs may need about 10 V.

P.title: tr-transistors.q1.q
Electronics: What does a gate pull-down resistor do?

P.title: tr-transistors.q1.o1
Electronics: Keeps the MOSFET off when the pin is floating

P.title: tr-transistors.q1.x
Electronics: It holds the gate at 0 V during boot.

P.title: tr-transistors.q2.q
Electronics: A MOSFET with 50 mΩ carries 4 A. Its heat is…

P.title: tr-transistors.c0.text
Electronics: A microcontroller pin can only supply a few milliamps. A motor, LED strip or relay needs far more. A transistor lets the small pin current control a much larger load current.

P.title: tr-transistors.c1.text
Electronics: In a bipolar transistor (NPN), a small current into the base lets a much larger current flow from collector to emitter. The ratio, the gain (hFE), is often 100 or more.

P.title: tr-transistors.c2.text
Electronics: A MOSFET is controlled by the voltage on its gate, with almost no gate current. When fully on, its resistance can be just milliohms, so it barely heats up. Most power switching uses MOSFETs.

P.title: tr-transistors.c3.text
Electronics: The simplest way: put an N-channel MOSFET between the load and ground. The pin drives the gate; when it's high, the load's ground path closes.

P.title: tr-transistors.c4.text
Electronics: Many MOSFETs need 10 V on the gate to switch fully on. With a 3.3 V microcontroller, choose a logic-level MOSFET specified to be fully on at 2.5–3.3 V, such as the AO3400 or IRLZ44N.

P.title: tr-transistors.c4.viz.items.1.r
Electronics: it's only half on, check gate voltage

P.title: tr-transistors.c5.text
Electronics: Add a small resistor (around 100 Ω) between pin and gate to limit current spikes, and a 10 kΩ pull-down from gate to ground so the MOSFET stays off while the microcontroller boots.

P.title: tr-transistors.c6.text
Electronics: Between fully off and fully on, a transistor can amplify: a small varying signal at the input gives a larger copy at the output. That's how radios and audio amplifiers work.

P.title: tr-transistors.c7.text
Electronics: Power lost in a switching MOSFET is I² × R(on). A MOSFET with 20 mΩ carrying 10 A loses 2 W, which needs a small heatsink. Switching fast also matters, because power is lost during each transition.

P.title: tr-transistors.c8.text
Electronics: An optocoupler passes a signal through light inside a sealed chip, isolating two circuits electrically. Solid-state relays use the same idea to switch mains loads silently, without moving parts.

P.title: tr-transistors.c9.text
Electronics: Modern processors contain tens of billions of microscopic MOSFETs acting as switches. The same device that drives your LED strip, shrunk to a few nanometres, does all the computing.

P.title: tr-opamps.summary
Electronics: The Swiss army knife of analog electronics.

P.title: tr-opamps.q0.q
Electronics: A non-inverting amplifier with Rf = 4 kΩ and Rg = 1 kΩ has a gain of…

P.title: tr-opamps.q1.q
Electronics: What does a voltage follower do?

P.title: tr-opamps.q1.o1
Electronics: Buffers a weak signal with a gain of 1

P.title: tr-opamps.q1.x
Electronics: It isolates the source from the load.

P.title: tr-opamps.q2.q
Electronics: Without feedback, an op-amp acts as…

P.title: tr-opamps.q2.x
Electronics: It just shows which input is higher.

P.title: tr-opamps.c0.text
Electronics: An operational amplifier is a chip with two inputs (+ and −) and one output. It amplifies the difference between the inputs by an enormous factor, often 100,000 times or more.

P.title: tr-opamps.c1.text
Electronics: On its own, that huge gain is unusable. Feeding part of the output back to the minus input sets a precise, stable gain chosen by two resistors.

P.title: tr-opamps.c2.text
Electronics: The classic way to boost a small sensor signal. The output follows the input, multiplied by a gain set by two resistors.

P.title: tr-opamps.c3.text
Electronics: Connect the output straight to the minus input and the gain is 1. Useless? No: it isolates a weak source from a heavy load, a "buffer".

P.title: tr-opamps.c4.text
Electronics: Without feedback, an op-amp (or a dedicated comparator chip) just tells you which input is higher: output high or low. Great for thermostats and light-activated switches.

P.title: tr-opamps.c5.text
Electronics: With negative feedback, analyse op-amp circuits with two rules: no current flows into the inputs, and the output does whatever it takes to make both inputs equal.

P.title: tr-opamps.c6.text
Electronics: Older op-amps can't swing their output close to the supply rails. On 3.3 V or 5 V circuits, choose a rail-to-rail op-amp so the signal can use the full range.

P.title: tr-opamps.c6.viz.l.items.1
Electronics: output stops short of the rails

P.title: tr-opamps.c6.viz.r.items.1
Electronics: output reaches near 0 V and 3.3 V

P.title: tr-opamps.c7.text
Electronics: With capacitors, op-amps make active filters: low-pass to remove noise from a sensor, high-pass to block DC, band-pass for a specific frequency.

P.title: tr-opamps.c8.text
Electronics: Op-amps can add several signals (audio mixers) or subtract one from another (measuring the small voltage across a current-sense resistor).

P.title: tr-opamps.c9.text
Electronics: The μA741, introduced in 1968, became the most famous op-amp ever made and is still taught today, though modern parts are far better for low-voltage circuits.

P.title: tr-psu.summary
Electronics: Getting the right voltage, cleanly and efficiently.

P.title: tr-psu.q0.q
Electronics: A linear regulator drops 9 V to 5 V at 0.2 A. How much heat?

P.title: tr-psu.q1.q
Electronics: Which is most efficient for 24 V down to 3.3 V?

P.title: tr-psu.q2.q
Electronics: An adapter rated 2 A powers a project drawing 0.5 A. Is that OK?

P.title: tr-psu.q2.o0
Electronics: Yes, it only draws what it needs

P.title: tr-psu.q2.x
Electronics: The rating is a maximum, not what's forced in.

P.title: tr-psu.c0.text
Electronics: Batteries sag as they discharge, and USB can vary between about 4.75 and 5.25 V. Chips want a steady voltage, so a regulator holds it constant whatever the input does.

P.title: tr-psu.c1.text
Electronics: A linear regulator (such as an LM7805 or AMS1117) burns off the extra voltage as heat. Simple and quiet, but wasteful when the input is much higher than the output.

P.title: tr-psu.c2.text
Electronics: A low-dropout (LDO) regulator works with input only slightly above output, for example 3.6 V in for 3.3 V out. Essential when running from a single lithium cell.

P.title: tr-psu.c3.text
Electronics: A buck converter steps voltage down by switching on and off very fast through an inductor. Efficiency of 85–95% means little heat, even from 24 V to 3.3 V.

P.title: tr-psu.c4.text
Electronics: A boost converter steps voltage up, such as from a 3.7 V battery to 5 V for USB. It draws more current from the battery than it delivers at the output.

P.title: tr-psu.c5.text
Electronics: For a large drop, switching regulators win. For small drops and noise-sensitive analog circuits, an LDO can be better.

P.title: tr-psu.c6.text
Electronics: Switching regulators leave a small ripple at their switching frequency. Sensitive circuits (audio, precise ADCs) use extra filtering or an LDO after the buck converter.

P.title: tr-psu.c7.text
Electronics: Match the voltage exactly, make sure the current rating is at least what your project needs, and check polarity of the barrel plug. A higher current rating is fine: the device only draws what it needs.

P.title: tr-psu.c8.text
Electronics: USB-C PD negotiates higher voltages, 9, 15 or 20 V, up to 100 W or more, but only after a digital handshake. A plain USB-C cable without negotiation gives 5 V.

P.title: tr-psu.c9.text
Electronics: If the supply dips below what a chip needs, it can misbehave or reset. ESP32s are famous for resetting on Wi-Fi transmit bursts with a weak supply. A good regulator and a big capacitor near the board fix it.

P.title: tr-psu.c9.viz.items.0.r
Electronics: stronger 3.3 V supply and a 470 µF capacitor near the board

P.title: tr-sensors.summary
Electronics: Measuring temperature, distance, motion and more.

P.title: tr-sensors.q0.q
Electronics: An ultrasonic echo returns after 2.9 ms. The distance is about…

P.title: tr-sensors.q1.q
Electronics: Why can a PIR sensor miss someone sitting still?

P.title: tr-sensors.q1.o1
Electronics: It detects changes in infrared heat from movement

P.title: tr-sensors.q2.o1
Electronics: AC current without cutting the wire

P.title: tr-sensors.c0.text
Electronics: A sensor turns a physical quantity into an electrical signal: a voltage, a resistance, a pulse length or digital data. The microcontroller reads it and converts it to real units.

P.title: tr-sensors.c1.text
Electronics: Thermistors change resistance with temperature (cheap, analog). The DS18B20 sends digital readings on one wire. The BME280 adds humidity and pressure over I²C.

P.title: tr-sensors.c2.text
Electronics: Sensors like the HC-SR04 and the waterproof JSN-SR04T send a 40 kHz ping and time the echo. Distance is half the round trip times the speed of sound.

P.title: tr-sensors.c2.viz.items.1.m
Electronics: m/s speed of sound in air

P.title: tr-sensors.c3.text
Electronics: Speed of sound changes with temperature (about 0.6 m/s per °C), so add temperature compensation for accuracy. The JSN-SR04T has a blind zone of roughly 20–25 cm and needs a clear path.

P.title: tr-sensors.c4.text
Electronics: PIR sensors detect the infrared heat of moving people and animals. Microwave radar sensors detect motion through thin walls and even breathing; they're used for presence detection.

P.title: tr-sensors.c5.text
Electronics: A photoresistor (LDR) is cheap and slow; the BH1750 gives calibrated lux readings over I²C. Useful for automatic lights and blinds.

P.title: tr-sensors.c6.text
Electronics: A current transformer clamp measures AC current without cutting wires; modules like the PZEM-004T report voltage, current, power and energy. INA219 boards measure DC current and voltage.

P.title: tr-sensors.c7.text
Electronics: Analog sensors give a voltage you read with the ADC; noise and calibration are your problem. Digital sensors do the conversion inside and send a number over I²C, SPI or one-wire.

P.title: tr-sensors.c8.text
Electronics: Cheap sensors have offsets and drift. Compare with a trusted reference at two points (for example ice water and room temperature) and correct in software.

P.title: tr-sensors.c9.text
Electronics: Take several readings and average them, or use a median to ignore outliers. Don't sample faster than you need: it wastes power and adds noise.

P.title: tr-sensors.c9.viz.items.2
Electronics: Sample only as often as needed

P.title: tr-buses.q0.q
Electronics: Which bus uses SDA and SCL lines?

P.title: tr-buses.q0.x
Electronics: I²C uses data and clock lines.

P.title: tr-buses.q1.q
Electronics: In UART wiring, TX connects to…

P.title: tr-buses.q2.q
Electronics: What's best for a 300 m cable to an energy meter?

P.title: tr-buses.q2.x
Electronics: RS-485 is differential and handles long runs.

P.title: tr-buses.c0.text
Electronics: Sensors, displays and memory chips need to exchange data with the microcontroller. Standard serial buses send bits one after another over a few wires.

P.title: tr-buses.c1.text
Electronics: UART uses a TX line and an RX line, crossed between devices (TX to RX). Both sides must agree on the speed, such as 9600 or 115200 baud. GPS modules and serial consoles use it.

P.title: tr-buses.c2.text
Electronics: I²C uses two lines, SDA (data) and SCL (clock), shared by many devices. Each device has an address, such as 0x76 for a BME280. Both lines need pull-up resistors.

P.title: tr-buses.c3.text
Electronics: SPI uses a clock, data out, data in and a chip-select line per device. It's fast, often tens of MHz, so it's used for displays, SD cards and flash memory.

P.title: tr-buses.c4.text
Electronics: I²C for many slow sensors on two wires; SPI for speed; UART for modules with their own protocol; one-wire for long chains of temperature sensors.

P.title: tr-buses.c5.text
Electronics: Two I²C devices with the same address can't share a bus. Many boards have a jumper to change the address, or you can use an I²C multiplexer.

P.title: tr-buses.c5.viz.items.0.r
Electronics: change one to 0x77 with its address jumper

P.title: tr-buses.c6.text
Electronics: When an I²C device doesn't respond, run a scanner sketch that tries every address and lists what answers. No answer usually means wiring, power or missing pull-ups.

P.title: tr-buses.c7.text
Electronics: I²C was designed for short connections on one board; beyond about a metre it becomes unreliable. For longer runs use RS-485, CAN or a differential bus extender.

P.title: tr-buses.c8.text
Electronics: RS-485 sends data as the difference between two wires, which rejects noise over long cables. Industrial devices, energy meters and solar inverters often speak Modbus over RS-485.

P.title: tr-buses.c9.text
Electronics: A cheap USB logic analyser records the bits on a bus and decodes them into readable bytes, showing exactly what's being sent. It's the fastest way to debug a stubborn sensor.

P.title: tr-wireless.summary
Electronics: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee and LoRa compared.

P.title: tr-wireless.q0.q
Electronics: Which suits a battery sensor sending a reading every 10 minutes from 5 km away?

P.title: tr-wireless.q0.x
Electronics: LoRa offers long range at very low power.

P.title: tr-wireless.q1.q
Electronics: In a Zigbee mesh, what extends range?

P.title: tr-wireless.q2.q
Electronics: What frequency does LoRa use in Europe?

P.title: tr-wireless.c0.text
Electronics: Every wireless technology balances range, data rate and power use. You can't max out all three: long range and low power means very little data.

P.title: tr-wireless.c1.text
Electronics: Wi-Fi offers high speed and connects directly to your network and the internet, but uses a lot of power. Good for mains-powered devices like cameras and smart plugs.

P.title: tr-wireless.c2.text
Electronics: BLE sends small amounts of data over short distances with very little power. Fitness bands, sensors and beacons use it, often running for a year or more on a coin cell.

P.title: tr-wireless.c3.text
Electronics: Mesh networks for smart homes: each mains-powered device relays messages, extending range. They need a hub or coordinator, and battery sensors last years.

P.title: tr-wireless.c4.text
Electronics: LoRa uses a special chirp signal to reach several kilometres with tiny power. Data rates are only hundreds of bits to a few kilobits per second: perfect for occasional sensor readings at remote sites.

P.title: tr-wireless.c5.text
Electronics: LoRa is the radio. LoRaWAN is a network protocol with gateways and servers, like The Things Network. Point-to-point LoRa between two boards needs no network at all.

P.title: tr-wireless.c6.text
Electronics: LoRa in Europe uses the 868 MHz licence-free band, with duty-cycle limits (often 1%), so each device may only transmit a small share of the time.

P.title: tr-wireless.c7.text
Electronics: A good antenna, mounted high and clear of metal, often doubles range more cheaply than more power. Never transmit without an antenna connected: it can damage the radio.

P.title: tr-wireless.c8.text
Electronics: Radio waves at these frequencies are blocked by hills, buildings and water. In the countryside, raising the antenna a few metres can turn no signal into a solid link.

P.title: tr-wireless.c9.text
Electronics: Where there's no Wi-Fi or gateway, LTE-M and NB-IoT modules send small amounts of data through the mobile network with low power, for a monthly SIM fee.

P.title: tr-esphome.summary
Electronics: Building smart-home devices without writing much code.

P.title: tr-esphome.q0.q
Electronics: What does ESPHome use to describe a device?

P.title: tr-esphome.q1.q
Electronics: Why avoid ADC2 pins for analog readings on an ESP32?

P.title: tr-esphome.q1.o1
Electronics: They can't be read while Wi-Fi is active

P.title: tr-esphome.q2.q
Electronics: What does deep sleep give a battery device?

P.title: tr-esphome.q2.x
Electronics: The chip almost entirely powers down.

P.title: tr-esphome.c0.text
Electronics: A cheap microcontroller with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth built in, two cores at up to 240 MHz and dozens of GPIO pins. It's the heart of countless DIY smart-home devices.

P.title: tr-esphome.c1.text
Electronics: Instead of writing C++ code, you describe your device in a YAML file: which board, which sensors on which pins. ESPHome builds the firmware and connects it to Home Assistant.

P.title: tr-esphome.c2.text
Electronics: A few lines describe the board, Wi-Fi and a sensor: platform dht, pin GPIO4, name "Living room temperature", update interval 60 s. That's the whole program.

P.title: tr-esphome.c3.text
Electronics: After the first USB flash, ESPHome updates devices over Wi-Fi. Change the YAML, click install, and the device on the ceiling updates itself.

P.title: tr-esphome.c4.text
Electronics: ESPHome devices talk to Home Assistant through a fast native API, with encryption. Entities appear automatically, and automations can run on the device even if Home Assistant is down.

P.title: tr-esphome.c5.text
Electronics: ESPHome can talk to appliances over UART. Projects like MitsubishiCN105ESPHome connect an ESP32 to the CN105 port of a Mitsubishi air conditioner for local control without the cloud.

P.title: tr-esphome.c6.text
Electronics: Some ESP32 pins are input-only (34–39), some affect boot (0, 2, 12, 15), and ADC2 pins can't be used for analog readings while Wi-Fi is on. Check a pinout before wiring.

P.title: tr-esphome.c6.viz.items.0.w
Electronics: analog sensor on an ADC2 pin

P.title: tr-esphome.c6.viz.items.1.r
Electronics: move it to a safe pin

P.title: tr-esphome.c7.text
Electronics: Battery devices can wake up, take a reading, send it and go back to deep sleep for minutes. A deep-sleep ESP32 draws microamps instead of tens of milliamps.

P.title: tr-esphome.c8.text
Electronics: The family keeps growing: ESP32-S3 adds AI instructions and USB, ESP32-C3 is a low-cost RISC-V version, ESP32-C6 adds Wi-Fi 6 and Thread/Zigbee radio.

P.title: tr-esphome.c9.text
Electronics: ESPHome devices work entirely on your network, with no cloud account. If the internet goes down, your sensors and switches keep working.

P.title: tr-proto.summary
Electronics: Prototyping, soldering and making it permanent.

P.title: tr-proto.q0.q
Electronics: Where should you feed the solder?

P.title: tr-proto.q0.x
Electronics: The joint must be hot enough to melt it.

P.title: tr-proto.q1.q
Electronics: A dull, lumpy joint is usually…

P.title: tr-proto.c0.text
Electronics: A breadboard lets you build circuits without soldering. Holes in each short row of five are connected; the long rails along the sides carry power and ground.

P.title: tr-proto.c1.text
Electronics: Breadboards are great for testing but contacts get loose and add resistance. If a circuit behaves strangely, push the wires in again before rewriting your code.

P.title: tr-proto.c1.viz.items.0
Electronics: Check every wire is pushed in

P.title: tr-proto.c2.text
Electronics: Heat the joint (pad and wire together) with the iron, then feed solder into the joint, not onto the iron. A good joint is shiny and shaped like a small volcano.

P.title: tr-proto.c3.text
Electronics: For common lead-free solder, around 330–370 °C works well; leaded solder melts lower. Too cold gives dull, grainy joints; too hot burns pads and flux.

P.title: tr-proto.c4.text
Electronics: A cold joint looks dull and lumpy and may crack. A bridge connects two pads by accident. Too little solder leaves a weak joint. Desoldering braid or a pump fixes most mistakes.

P.title: tr-proto.c5.text
Electronics: Perfboard (stripboard) makes a project permanent without designing a PCB: components soldered in a grid, connected with wire or copper strips.

P.title: tr-proto.c6.text
Electronics: Free tools like KiCad let you draw the schematic and then the board layout. Upload the files to a PCB maker and boards arrive in about a week for a few euros.

P.title: tr-proto.c7.text
Electronics: Most modern parts are surface-mount (SMD): tiny, soldered onto pads rather than through holes. Sizes like 0805 are manageable by hand; smaller ones need hot air or a reflow oven.

P.title: tr-proto.c8.text
Electronics: Projects need a box: IP-rated enclosures for outdoors, 3D-printed cases for custom fits. Plan for cable glands, ventilation and antenna placement outside metal boxes.

P.title: tr-proto.c9.text
Electronics: Use a stand for the iron, ventilate or use fume extraction (flux fumes irritate the lungs), wash hands after handling solder, and wear eye protection when clipping leads.

P.title: tr-logic.summary
Electronics: Bits, gates and how chips make decisions.

P.title: tr-logic.q1.q
Electronics: An AND gate with inputs 1 and 0 outputs…

P.title: tr-logic.q2.x
Electronics: Two hex F's are eight 1 bits = 255.

P.title: tr-logic.c0.text
Electronics: Digital electronics represents everything with bits: 0 or 1, low or high voltage. Eight bits make a byte, which can hold 256 different values.

P.title: tr-logic.c1.text
Electronics: Each binary place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16… The number 1011 is 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.

P.title: tr-logic.c2.text
Electronics: Hex groups four bits into one digit, 0–9 then A–F. One byte is exactly two hex digits: 0xFF = 255. Addresses and colours (#FF8800) use hex.

P.title: tr-logic.c3.text
Electronics: The basic gates: AND outputs 1 only if all inputs are 1; OR outputs 1 if any input is 1; NOT flips the input.

P.title: tr-logic.c3.viz.l.items.1
Electronics: door open AND alarm armed → siren

P.title: tr-logic.c3.viz.r.items.1
Electronics: button A OR button B → light

P.title: tr-logic.c4.text
Electronics: Any logic circuit, even a whole processor, can be built from NAND gates alone (AND followed by NOT). It's cheap to make in silicon, so it's everywhere.

P.title: tr-logic.c5.text
Electronics: Exclusive OR outputs 1 when the inputs differ. It's used for adding binary numbers, parity checks and simple encryption.

P.title: tr-logic.c6.text
Electronics: A half adder adds two bits using XOR (for the sum) and AND (for the carry). Chain full adders together and you can add numbers of any size.

P.title: tr-logic.c7.text
Electronics: Feed two gates back into each other and the circuit remembers its last state. That's a flip-flop, the basis of registers and fast memory.

P.title: tr-logic.c8.text
Electronics: Digital circuits move in step with a clock signal ticking millions or billions of times a second. On each tick, flip-flops capture new values.

P.title: tr-logic.c9.text
Electronics: Programmers use bitwise operations to set, clear and test individual bits, for example in a register controlling GPIO pins: value | (1<<5) sets bit 5.

P.title: tr-memory.q0.q
Electronics: What happens to RAM contents when power is lost?

P.title: tr-memory.q1.q
Electronics: Why not write to flash every second?

P.title: tr-memory.q1.o1
Electronics: Flash cells wear out after many erase cycles

P.title: tr-memory.c0.text
Electronics: RAM holds the data a program is working on right now. It's fast but volatile: switch off the power and it's gone.

P.title: tr-memory.c1.text
Electronics: SRAM stores each bit in a flip-flop: fast, used for caches and microcontroller memory. DRAM stores bits as charge in tiny capacitors: denser and cheaper, used for computer RAM, but must be refreshed constantly.

P.title: tr-memory.c1.viz.items.2.b
Electronics: DRAM rewrites itself thousands of times a second

P.title: tr-memory.c2.text
Electronics: Flash keeps data without power by trapping charge in insulated cells. Your microcontroller's program, SSDs, SD cards and USB sticks all use it.

P.title: tr-memory.c3.text
Electronics: Each flash cell survives a limited number of erase cycles, from about 10,000 to 100,000 for small chips. Writing a log line every second to the same spot will kill it; wear levelling spreads writes around.

P.title: tr-memory.c3.viz.items.0.w
Electronics: write sensor data to flash every second

P.title: tr-memory.c3.viz.items.0.r
Electronics: keep it in RAM, write in batches

P.title: tr-memory.c4.text
Electronics: EEPROM can rewrite single bytes and is great for small settings like calibration values. On the ESP32 it's emulated in flash, with a library that handles it.

P.title: tr-memory.c5.text
Electronics: A classic ESP32 has about 520 KB of SRAM and usually 4 MB of flash. Variants with PSRAM add several MB of extra RAM, handy for cameras and displays.

P.title: tr-memory.c6.text
Electronics: Programs use two areas of RAM: the stack for function calls and local variables, the heap for memory requested at runtime. On small devices, fragmenting the heap with many strings can crash the program after hours.

P.title: tr-memory.c7.text
Electronics: Computers balance speed and size: tiny, ultra-fast registers and caches near the CPU, then RAM, then SSDs, then hard disks or the cloud.

P.title: tr-memory.c8.text
Electronics: For long-term data logging, an SD card over SPI offers gigabytes of storage. Write in blocks, close files properly, and expect cheap cards to fail eventually.

P.title: tr-memory.c9.text
Electronics: A kilobyte is 1,000 bytes in SI units, but operating systems often count 1,024 (properly a kibibyte, KiB). That's why a "1 TB" drive shows up as about 931 GB.

P.title: tr-motors.q0.q
Electronics: What lets a DC motor run in both directions?

P.title: tr-motors.q0.x
Electronics: It reverses current with four switches.

P.title: tr-motors.q1.q
Electronics: A 1.5 ms servo pulse usually means…

P.title: tr-motors.q2.q
Electronics: Why might an ESP32 reset when a motor starts?

P.title: tr-motors.q2.o1
Electronics: Supply dips from the motor's start-up current

P.title: tr-motors.q2.x
Electronics: Use a separate supply and capacitors.

P.title: tr-motors.c0.title
Electronics: Never drive a motor from a pin

P.title: tr-motors.c0.text
Electronics: A small DC motor can draw hundreds of milliamps, more at start-up, and makes electrical noise. Always use a driver: a transistor, MOSFET or motor driver chip, plus a flyback diode.

P.title: tr-motors.c1.text
Electronics: An H-bridge uses four switches to reverse the current through a motor, so it can spin both ways. Chips like the L298N, DRV8833 or TB6612 do it for you.

P.title: tr-motors.c2.text
Electronics: Feed PWM into the motor driver and the motor spins at a speed set by the duty cycle. Frequencies of several kHz to 20+ kHz avoid audible whining.

P.title: tr-motors.c3.text
Electronics: When a motor is blocked or starting, it draws its stall current, often 5–10 times the running current. Size the driver and supply for it.

P.title: tr-motors.c4.text
Electronics: A hobby servo has a motor, gearbox and position sensor in one box. You send a pulse every 20 ms; its width, 1 to 2 ms, sets the angle from 0° to 180°.

P.title: tr-motors.c5.text
Electronics: A stepper moves in fixed steps, typically 200 per revolution (1.8° each). Drivers like the A4988 or TMC2209 take step and direction pulses and can microstep for smoother motion.

P.title: tr-motors.c5.viz.f
Electronics: steps per mm = (steps/rev × microsteps) ÷ mm per rev

P.title: tr-motors.c6.text
Electronics: Brushless DC motors (drones, fans, e-bikes) need an electronic speed controller (ESC) that switches three phases in sequence. They're efficient and long-lasting.

P.title: tr-motors.c7.text
Electronics: Power motors from their own supply, not from the microcontroller's 3.3 V regulator, and connect the grounds. Add capacitors near the motor driver to absorb spikes.

P.title: tr-motors.c7.viz.items.0.w
Electronics: motor on the ESP32 3.3 V pin

P.title: tr-motors.c7.viz.items.1.r
Electronics: add bulk capacitor near the driver

P.title: tr-motors.c8.text
Electronics: An encoder on the motor shaft counts pulses as it turns, so the controller knows the exact position and speed. With feedback, a cheap DC motor becomes a precise actuator.

P.title: tr-motors.c9.text
Electronics: A PID controller adjusts output based on the error now (P), accumulated past error (I) and how fast the error is changing (D). It keeps motors, heaters and drones steady.

P.title: tr-power.summary
Electronics: Making a battery last for months or years.

P.title: tr-power.q0.q
Electronics: What matters most for battery life in a device that sleeps 99% of the time?

P.title: tr-power.q1.q
Electronics: A 2,000 mAh battery and 0.5 mA average current lasts about…

P.title: tr-power.q2.q
Electronics: How can you reduce the energy of each Wi-Fi wake-up?

P.title: tr-power.q2.o1
Electronics: Use a static IP and fixed channel to connect faster

P.title: tr-power.c0.text
Electronics: Battery life = capacity ÷ average current. A device that wakes for 1 second every 10 minutes spends 99.8% of its time asleep, so sleep current matters enormously.

P.title: tr-power.c1.text
Electronics: Weight each state by how long it lasts.

P.title: tr-power.c1.example.0
Electronics: 2 s at 120 mA, 598 s at 10 µA, per 600 s

P.title: tr-power.c1.viz.f
Electronics: I avg = (I awake × t awake + I sleep × t sleep) ÷ t total

P.title: tr-power.c2.text
Electronics: An ESP32 draws about 100+ mA with Wi-Fi on but only around 10 µA in deep sleep (on a well-designed board). A timer, a pin or a sensor can wake it.

P.title: tr-power.c3.text
Electronics: Many dev boards waste power: a power LED, a USB-serial chip and an inefficient regulator can draw several mA even when the chip sleeps. For battery projects, choose a low-power board or remove the LED.

P.title: tr-power.c4.text
Electronics: Sensors draw current too. Power them from a GPIO pin or a MOSFET switch, turn them on just before reading, and off afterwards.

P.title: tr-power.c5.text
Electronics: Connecting to Wi-Fi can take seconds. Using a static IP, a fixed channel and saved credentials can cut it to under a second, saving a lot of energy per wake-up.

P.title: tr-power.c6.text
Electronics: For frequent readings over long distances on battery, LoRa or BLE use far less energy per message than Wi-Fi.

P.title: tr-power.c7.text
Electronics: Li-ion cells give 3.0–4.2 V and recharge; LiFePO4 is safer at 3.2 V nominal; primary lithium (like AA lithium or Li-SOCl₂) suits years without recharging in the cold.

P.title: tr-power.c8.text
Electronics: A small solar panel and charge controller can keep a remote sensor running indefinitely. Size the panel for winter, when sun is weakest, with some margin for cloudy weeks.

P.title: tr-power.c9.text
Electronics: Use a multimeter in series, or better a power profiler, to measure sleep and active currents. Small surprises like a floating pin or a pull-up can drain a battery in weeks.

P.title: tr-power.c9.viz.items.3
Electronics: Log battery voltage in your data

P.title: tr-datasheets.q0.o1
Electronics: Limits that must never be exceeded

P.title: tr-datasheets.q0.x
Electronics: Exceeding them can damage the part.

P.title: tr-datasheets.q1.q
Electronics: Two wires labelled "SCL" in different places on a schematic are…

P.title: tr-datasheets.q1.x
Electronics: Net labels connect points with the same name.

P.title: tr-datasheets.q2.q
Electronics: Should you design using typical or worst-case values?

P.title: tr-datasheets.q2.x
Electronics: Guarantees are the min and max values.

P.title: tr-datasheets.c0.text
Electronics: The first page lists the key features: supply range, interface, accuracy, current. If it doesn't fit your project there, you can stop reading.

P.title: tr-datasheets.c1.text
Electronics: These are limits that must never be exceeded, even briefly, or the part may be damaged. They are not normal operating conditions.

P.title: tr-datasheets.c2.text
Electronics: Typical is what most parts do; min and max are guarantees. Design for the worst case, not the typical value.

P.title: tr-datasheets.c3.text
Electronics: The pinout diagram shows which pin does what, viewed from above (usually). Pin 1 is marked by a dot or notch. Mistakes here are the most common cause of dead boards.

P.title: tr-datasheets.c4.text
Electronics: Most datasheets show a typical application circuit with the exact capacitors and resistors to use. Copy it closely, especially for regulators and radios.

P.title: tr-datasheets.c5.text
Electronics: Learn the basic symbols: resistor (zigzag or box), capacitor (two plates), diode (triangle and bar), transistor, ground and supply arrows.

P.title: tr-datasheets.c6.text
Electronics: Large schematics don't draw every wire; they give wires names. Two points labelled "SDA" are connected even if no line joins them.

P.title: tr-datasheets.c7.text
Electronics: Graphs show how parameters change with temperature, voltage or load. A sensor accurate at 25 °C may drift at −10 °C; a regulator may sag at high current.

P.title: tr-datasheets.c8.text
Electronics: Chips can have known bugs, published in an errata document. If a feature misbehaves despite correct code, check the errata first.

P.title: tr-datasheets.c9.text
Electronics: Datasheets are free from the manufacturer's website and distributors like Mouser, DigiKey or LCSC. Search by the exact part number printed on the chip.

P.title: tr-scope.q0.q
Electronics: Why is triggering important on a scope?

P.title: tr-scope.q0.o1
Electronics: It gives a stable picture of repeating signals

P.title: tr-scope.q1.q
Electronics: What's dangerous about a scope's ground clip?

P.title: tr-scope.q1.o1
Electronics: It's tied to earth, so the wrong connection makes a short

P.title: tr-scope.c0.text
Electronics: A multimeter gives one number; an oscilloscope draws voltage against time, so you can see waveforms, glitches, noise and timing.

P.title: tr-scope.c1.text
Electronics: The vertical axis is volts per division; the horizontal is time per division. Adjust both until the signal fills the screen nicely.

P.title: tr-scope.c2.text
Electronics: The trigger tells the scope when to start drawing, such as when the voltage crosses 1.5 V going up. Without it, a repeating signal scrolls and blurs.

P.title: tr-scope.c3.text
Electronics: A scope's bandwidth limits how fast a signal it can show accurately. As a rule, choose bandwidth about five times the highest frequency you care about.

P.title: tr-scope.c4.text
Electronics: The scope's probe ground is connected to mains earth. Clipping it onto a point that isn't at ground potential, such as in a mains circuit, creates a short circuit. Use isolated or differential probes for mains.

P.title: tr-scope.c4.viz.items.0.w
Electronics: ground clip on a mains circuit

P.title: tr-scope.c5.text
Electronics: Work from power outward: check supply voltages, then clocks, then signals. Change one thing at a time and note results.

P.title: tr-scope.c5.viz.steps.3
Electronics: Change one thing at a time

P.title: tr-scope.c6.text
Electronics: Printing values over the serial port is the cheapest debugger: what's the sensor reading, which branch did the code take, how long did it take?

P.title: tr-scope.c7.text
Electronics: Explaining the problem step by step, even to a rubber duck or a colleague, often reveals the mistake. Writing it down works too.

P.title: tr-scope.c8.text
Electronics: Many faults are simple: no common ground, swapped TX/RX, wrong voltage, loose breadboard wire, missing pull-up, or the wrong board selected in the IDE.

P.title: tr-scope.c9.text
Electronics: A €10 logic analyser, a basic multimeter and a USB oscilloscope or a used bench scope cover most hobby debugging.

P.title: tr-scope.c9.viz.items.3
Electronics: Bench power supply with current limit

P.title: tr-noise.summary
Electronics: Why circuits misbehave and how to calm them.

P.title: tr-noise.q0.q
Electronics: Where should a 100 nF decoupling capacitor go?

P.title: tr-noise.q0.o1
Electronics: Right next to the chip's power pins

P.title: tr-noise.q0.x
Electronics: Short distance means fast local supply.

P.title: tr-noise.q1.o1
Electronics: Rapid on-off flickering around a threshold

P.title: tr-noise.q2.q
Electronics: Why use twisted pair for long sensor cables?

P.title: tr-noise.q2.o1
Electronics: Noise is picked up equally on both wires and cancels

P.title: tr-noise.c0.text
Electronics: Every chip needs a small capacitor (typically 100 nF) right next to its power pins. When the chip suddenly draws current, the capacitor supplies it locally, preventing dips on the rail.

P.title: tr-noise.c1.text
Electronics: Besides small decoupling caps, add a larger electrolytic or ceramic (10–470 µF) where power enters the board and near motors or radios, to absorb slower dips.

P.title: tr-noise.c2.text
Electronics: If two parts of a system are grounded at different points with different potentials, current flows through the ground wires, causing hum in audio or errors in sensors.

P.title: tr-noise.c3.text
Electronics: Bring grounds from noisy parts (motors, power) and sensitive parts (sensors) back to one point separately, so noisy currents don't flow through sensitive ground paths.

P.title: tr-noise.c4.text
Electronics: Long wires act as antennas. Use twisted pairs, shielded cable, lower impedance signals, or digital and differential signals for long runs.

P.title: tr-noise.c4.viz.items.1
Electronics: Shielded cable, shield grounded at one end

P.title: tr-noise.c5.text
Electronics: An unconnected input picks up noise and reads random values, and can even increase power use. Always define its level with a pull-up or pull-down.

P.title: tr-noise.c6.text
Electronics: Even with good hardware, readings may jitter. Median filters remove spikes; moving averages smooth noise; hysteresis stops thresholds from flickering.

P.title: tr-noise.c7.text
Electronics: A thermostat set at 20 °C would click on and off constantly around 20. With hysteresis it turns on at 19.5 and off at 20.5. ESPHome and Home Assistant thermostats support this.

P.title: tr-noise.c8.text
Electronics: Buck converters and motors create fast edges that radiate noise. Keep their loops small, place input capacitors close, and separate them from analog circuits.

P.title: tr-noise.c9.text
Electronics: Commercial products must pass electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) tests: they mustn't emit too much interference or be upset by it. The CE mark in Europe covers this.

P.title: tr-displays.summary
Electronics: Lighting things up, from one LED to a screen.

P.title: tr-displays.q0.q
Electronics: How much current can 100 WS2812B LEDs draw at full white?

P.title: tr-displays.q1.q
Electronics: Which display keeps its image with no power?

P.title: tr-displays.q2.q
Electronics: Red light plus green light appears…

P.title: tr-displays.c0.text
Electronics: LED brightness depends on current, so LEDs are driven with a resistor or a constant-current driver, never straight from a voltage source.

P.title: tr-displays.c1.text
Electronics: WS2812B ("NeoPixel") strips contain a tiny controller in every LED. One data wire sets the colour of each LED individually, perfect for effects controlled by an ESP32.

P.title: tr-displays.c2.text
Electronics: Each WS2812B can draw about 60 mA at full white. Long strips need thick wires and power injected at several points.

P.title: tr-displays.c2.example.2
Electronics: ≈ 18 A at full white: big 5 V supply

P.title: tr-displays.c3.text
Electronics: WS2812B strips at 5 V may not reliably read a 3.3 V data signal from an ESP32. A simple level shifter (like a 74AHCT125) or a sacrificial first LED fixes flicker.

P.title: tr-displays.c3.viz.items.0.r
Electronics: level shifter on the data line

P.title: tr-displays.c3.viz.items.1.r
Electronics: add a 330 Ω resistor and keep it short

P.title: tr-displays.c4.text
Electronics: The classic 16×2 LCD shows two lines of text. With an I²C backpack, it needs only four wires.

P.title: tr-displays.c5.text
Electronics: Small OLED screens (like 0.96" SSD1306, 128×64) give crisp graphics with no backlight. Each pixel emits light, so black uses no power. Static images can burn in over time.

P.title: tr-displays.c6.text
Electronics: E-paper displays keep their image with zero power, like a Kindle. They refresh slowly, but are perfect for battery-powered dashboards updated every few minutes.

P.title: tr-displays.c7.text
Electronics: To drive many LEDs with few pins, light them rows at a time very quickly. Persistence of vision makes the display look steady.

P.title: tr-displays.c7.viz.steps.3
Electronics: Repeat hundreds of times a second

P.title: tr-displays.c8.text
Electronics: RGB LEDs mix red, green and blue light. Full red + green looks yellow; all three at full make white.

P.title: tr-displays.c9.text
Electronics: ESPHome supports many displays: show temperatures, clocks or Home Assistant states with a few lines of configuration and a lambda for drawing.

P.title: tr-computer.q0.q
Electronics: What are the steps of the CPU cycle?

P.title: tr-computer.q0.x
Electronics: The core loop of every processor.

P.title: tr-computer.q1.o1
Electronics: To keep frequently used data close and fast

P.title: tr-computer.q1.x
Electronics: RAM is slow compared with the CPU.

P.title: tr-computer.q2.q
Electronics: Which instruction set is open and used in the ESP32-C3?

P.title: tr-computer.c0.text
Electronics: A processor repeats one cycle billions of times a second: fetch an instruction from memory, decode it, execute it, and move on.

P.title: tr-computer.c1.text
Electronics: Each instruction does something tiny: add two numbers, compare them, load from memory, jump to another instruction. Everything complex is built from millions of these.

P.title: tr-computer.c2.text
Electronics: Registers are tiny, ultra-fast storage slots inside the CPU. The arithmetic logic unit (ALU) does the actual maths and logic on them.

P.title: tr-computer.c3.text
Electronics: You write code in a language like C++ or Python; a compiler or interpreter turns it into machine instructions the CPU understands.

P.title: tr-computer.c4.text
Electronics: Modern chips have several cores, each a complete processor, running separate tasks at the same time. The ESP32 has two; laptops have 8 or more.

P.title: tr-computer.c5.text
Electronics: Performance depends on instructions per clock, cache size, memory speed and parallelism, not just GHz. A newer 3 GHz chip can be much faster than an older 4 GHz one.

P.title: tr-computer.c6.text
Electronics: Fetching data from RAM takes a long time in CPU terms. Caches keep recently used data close to the core. Most programs reuse data, so caches hit most of the time.

P.title: tr-computer.c7.text
Electronics: An operating system shares the CPU, memory and devices between many programs, switching between them thousands of times a second so each seems to run continuously.

P.title: tr-computer.c8.text
Electronics: x86 dominates PCs and servers; ARM dominates phones and is spreading to laptops and data centres; RISC-V is an open instruction set growing in microcontrollers, like the ESP32-C3.

P.title: tr-computer.c9.text
Electronics: In 1965 Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors on a chip doubled about every two years. The trend held for decades, though it has slowed as transistors approach atomic sizes.
